title: Worksheet — Development (Class 10 CBSE Economics)
instructions: Attempt all 11 questions. Show your reasoning where required. Total time: 50 minutes.

questions.question: Per capita income is calculated as:
Which of these CANNOT be bought directly in the market?
options: a clean public school + safe streets + clean water
questions.answer: a clean public school + safe streets + clean water

questions.question: Per capita income alone is enough to compare development of countries.
The Human Development Report is published by the ____.
Among Kerala, Haryana and Bihar, which has the LOWEST IMR?
Reckless cutting of forests can cause ALL of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Forests AID recharge; cutting them reduces it.

questions.question: Why is per capita income preferred over total income for comparing countries? How does the World Bank classify countries by income?
questions.answer: Total income depends on population — comparing total incomes does not tell us how much each person earns on average. PER CAPITA INCOME (= total income ÷ population) gives the AVERAGE income per person and allows fair comparison across countries of different sizes. The World Bank classifies countries into HIGH-INCOME, LOW-INCOME and MIDDLE-INCOME, with thresholds revised over time. India is in the LOW-MIDDLE income group.
questions.explanation: Per capita rationale + World Bank groups.

questions.question: List THREE limitations of using per capita income alone as a measure of development.
questions.answer: (i) AVERAGE INCOME HIDES INEQUALITY — two countries with the same average can have very different distributions. (ii) Many things people care about — clean schools, safe streets, water, public hospitals — are PUBLIC FACILITIES that cannot be bought directly. (iii) NON-MATERIAL goals like health, education, freedom and security are not captured by income alone.

questions.question: Why is Kerala — though it has a LOWER per capita income than Haryana — said to have BETTER overall development? Use specific indicators.
questions.answer: Although Haryana has higher per capita income, Kerala does much better on HUMAN-DEVELOPMENT indicators: lower IMR (~7 vs ~30), higher literacy rate, higher net attendance in schools and higher life expectancy. This is because Kerala has invested more in PUBLIC HEALTH (primary health centres, immunisation) and PUBLIC EDUCATION (good public schools). Higher income alone does not guarantee a better life — how income is spent on collective goods matters at least as much.
questions.explanation: PCI vs HDI in Indian states.

questions.question: Discuss the importance of PUBLIC FACILITIES in development. Why are they essential for the poor? Give examples.
questions.answer: PUBLIC FACILITIES are services provided collectively by the government — schools, primary health centres, drinking water, electricity, public transport, sewage, parks. They are essential because (i) many things needed for a good life CANNOT be bought individually — clean air and water, public hospitals, parks; (ii) public facilities are MOST IMPORTANT FOR THE POOR — the rich can sometimes buy private alternatives, but the poor cannot, so good public facilities are their only path to good health and education; (iii) public facilities provide a LEVEL PLAYING FIELD; (iv) they raise the quality of life of those who 'don't need them' too — clean public hospitals and schools reduce disease and crime, benefiting everyone. Kerala — with lower PCI than Haryana — has better health and education outcomes BECAUSE of its strong public facilities.

questions.question: Why is sustainability a key concern in development? Discuss with at least three Indian / global examples.
questions.answer: SUSTAINABILITY is a concern because the resources we depend on are FINITE — but we are using them at a pace that leaves little for future generations. SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT means meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. EXAMPLES: (i) GROUNDWATER — India is the world's largest groundwater extractor. In Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and parts of Tamil Nadu, water is being pumped much faster than rains can refill the aquifer; wells are drying up. (ii) CRUDE OIL — at current consumption rates the world's reserves last about 35–40 years; we need a transition to renewable energy. (iii) FORESTS — reckless cutting reduces rainfall, harms biodiversity, increases erosion and warms the climate. (iv) CLIMATE CHANGE — environmental damage crosses national borders; countries must cooperate on climate, oceans and ozone. Any development that ignores SUSTAINABILITY is borrowing from our children — a debt no nation can pay back.
